desc.mast: Access the MAST archive (Kepler, K2, TESS, Hubble, JWST) with lightkurve and astroquery: star light curves, famous transits and TESS FFI images.
desc.meteors: Meteor showers: full calendar, peak dates, ZHR, radiants and best viewing times all year round — alerts the day before each peak on OrbitLight.
desc.asteroids: Asteroids: upcoming Earth close approaches, LD distances, hazardous objects and a live NASA NEO catalogue of near-Earth objects updated daily.
desc.events: Astronomy events: solar and lunar eclipses, planetary conjunctions, Moon phases, retrograde stations and a weekly event calendar on OrbitLight.
desc.launches: Rocket launches: schedule, missions, launch vehicles and livestreams — alerts at 24 h, 2 h and 30 min before each liftoff on OrbitLight.
desc.deep: Deep space: space-debris statistics, GCN gamma-ray bursts, Voyager distances, Mars weather and the latest news from beyond Earth orbit.
desc.voyager: Voyager 1 & 2: current distance, speed, light-time from Earth and the story of the interstellar mission — computed live on OrbitLight.
desc.comets: Comets: orbits, current positions, next close approaches to the Sun and Earth, telescope and naked-eye visibility — calendar on OrbitLight.
desc.exoplanets: Exoplanets: the latest TESS discoveries, sizes and orbits of planets around other stars, the habitable zone and detection methods on OrbitLight.
desc.rtl: Radio astronomy: meteor pings, Jupiter and solar spectra received on an SDR receiver.
desc.community: OrbitLight community: forum, photo gallery, observation diaries and local groups.
desc.gallery: NASA photo archive: the Astronomy Picture of the Day by date — Hubble, James Webb, probes and rovers with Ukrainian descriptions.
desc.galaxies: Famous galaxies: Andromeda, Whirlpool, Sombrero, M82, Centaurus A and more — live NASA/IPAC NED redshift and type data, photos from the NASA Image Library.
desc.planetarium: OrbitLight planetarium: every solar-system planet — diameter, day and year length, gravity, moons and mean temperature. Mars adds live weather and rover photos.
desc.mars: Mars weather from InSight, fresh Perseverance and Curiosity rover photos, Phobos and Deimos, Earth comparison, dust storms and the history of Mars exploration.
desc.jupiter: Jupiter up close: the Great Red Spot, the Galilean moons, a system of 95 moons, radiation, the Juno, Europa Clipper and JUICE missions and next opposition.
desc.mercury: Mercury up close: extreme temperature swings, the 3:2 spin-orbit resonance, Caloris Basin, the MESSENGER and BepiColombo missions and best times to observe.
desc.earth: The only planet known to host life: interior structure, atmosphere, magnetosphere, plate tectonics, the Earth-Moon system and Earth-observation satellites.
desc.venus: Venus up close: runaway greenhouse effect, sulfuric acid clouds, retrograde rotation, Magellan radar mapping and the Venera and Akatsuki missions.
desc.neptune: Neptune up close: the strongest winds in the system, dark spots, five faint rings, the retrograde moon Triton with cryovolcanoes, and a history discovered 'on paper'.
desc.uranus: Uranus up close: 98° axial tilt, coldest atmosphere, thirteen vertical rings, twenty-eight moons, and the single Voyager 2 flyby.
desc.saturn: Saturn up close: the Solar System's most spectacular rings, a hexagonal storm at the north pole, over 140 moons, the Cassini-Huygens and Dragonfly missions and the next opposition.
desc.news: The top spaceflight stories in Ukrainian — translated and summarized coverage from SpaceflightNow, NASA, ESA and other sources, updated daily.

storm.headline: Active geomagnetic storm

s1.title: Kp index
s1.sub: The planetary K-index (Kp) measures Earth's magnetic-field disturbance. Values ≥ 5 indicate a geomagnetic storm (G1–G5 scale).

s2.title: Plasma stream from the Sun
s2.sub: Solar-wind speed (DSCOVR/ACE) and the Bz component of the magnetic field. Southward Bz (< 0) «opens» the magnetosphere to aurora.

s3.title: X-ray flux (GOES)
s3.sub: Soft X-ray flux 0.1–0.8 nm. Classes: A < B < C < M < X (each step ×10). M- and X-class flares affect radio communications.

s4.title: Aurora forecast
s4.sub: NOAA OVATION aurora visibility map for the Northern Hemisphere — refreshed about every 5 minutes. The aurora chance for your latitude is computed from the current Kp.
s4.tip: The aurora is visible at Kp ≥ 6 in northern Ukraine and ≥ 8 across the whole country. Watch the northern horizon as far from city lights as possible.

s5.title: Weather on Mars

mars.whatBody: A sol is a Martian day (24 h 39 min). InSight measured temperature and pressure in Elysium crater for over two Martian years. The mission ended in December 2022 — the feed returns the last available sol.

hero.title: Meteor shower over your head
hero.sub: The year's most active meteor showers — peak dates, expected zenithal hourly rate (ZHR), radiant and best observing time. Active showers are highlighted live.

s1.title: Showers of this and next season
s1.sub: Showers are sorted by proximity to peak. ZHR is the zenithal hourly rate: how many meteors an ideal observer would see per hour under a clear, dark sky.

s2.title: How to watch a meteor shower

tips.t1_title: Look a bit off the radiant
tips.t1_body: Meteors are visible across the whole sky, but near the radiant their “trails” are shortest — better to look 30–60° away from it.
tips.t2_body: Get 20–30 km out of the city. Faint meteors vanish in light pollution first.
tips.t3_body: New Moon is ideal. A full Moon “washes out” everything but the brightest fireballs. The “For observer” page shows the phase.
tips.t4_title: Put the phone away and wait
tips.t4_body: Eyes need 20 minutes to adapt. Lie back in a chair, grab a blanket and count for at least an hour — ZHR is an estimate.

what.title: What is an eclipse?
what.body: A solar eclipse occurs when the Moon covers the Sun; a lunar eclipse when Earth casts its shadow on the Moon. A total solar eclipse is one of the most awe-inspiring celestial sights, but it is only visible from a narrow strip on Earth.

howto.h1_body: Even a bright comet is lost in city light pollution — get out of town or to a park far from streetlights.
howto.h2_body: The tail and coma open up better in 7×50 or 10×50 binoculars than in the narrow field of a telescope.
howto.h3_body: A bright Moon washes out a faint comet tail — pick days near new Moon.

hero.title: Deep space
hero.sub: Things beyond daily ISS passes: space debris around Earth, the most powerful explosions in the Universe — gamma-ray bursts, and the farthest human-made probes, Voyager, flying into interstellar space.

s1.title: Space debris
s1.sub: Everything orbiting Earth that is uncontrolled: spent upper stages, dead satellites, collision fragments. Even a 1-cm fragment at orbital velocity hits like a shell.

debris.whyBody: Debris breeds more debris: collisions cascade fragments (Kessler syndrome), threatening comms and navigation satellites.
debris.dataBody: Statistics from the ESA Space Environment Report {{year}}. Updated yearly.

s2.title: Gamma-ray bursts (GRB)
s2.sub: Gamma-ray bursts are the most energetic explosions in the Universe since the Big Bang: collapse of a massive star or merger of neutron stars. NASA GCN sends circulars to observers within minutes of an event.

grb.whatBody1: A GRB lasts from milliseconds to hundreds of seconds. In a few seconds it emits more energy than the Sun in a billion years. Light from the farthest GRBs takes billions of years to reach us.
grb.whatBody2: GCN (Gamma-ray Coordinates Network) relays the burst's coordinates to telescopes worldwide for rapid follow-up of the “afterglow”.

v1.title: Voyager 1 — the farthest human-made object
v1.body: Launched in 1977. The first probe in interstellar space (2017). Carries the “Golden Record” with a message for aliens.

v2.title: Voyager 2 — the only probe to visit all ice giants
v2.body: Flew past Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. Also in interstellar space (2018). Its signal takes over 18 hours to reach Earth.

hero.eyebrow: 49 years in flight · beyond the Solar System
hero.title:
The path taken by
Voyager 1 and 2
hero.sub: Two spacecraft launched in the summer of 1977 became the farthest human-made objects in history. Both have left the heliosphere and are flying through interstellar space, moving tens of kilometers farther every second.

legend.v1: Voyager 1 — course north of the ecliptic
legend.v2: Voyager 2 — course south of the ecliptic
legend.helio: Heliopause — the limit of the Sun's influence

cards.lightHours: ≈ {{n}} h of light travel to Earth

tl.t1_body: Voyager 2 launched first but on a slower trajectory — Voyager 1 caught up and overtook it before Jupiter.
tl.t2_body: Both probes discovered active volcanoes on Io and a thin ring around Jupiter.
tl.t3_body: Detailed images of the ring system; after this the probes' paths parted for good.
tl.t4_body: The only close-up images of these planets in history — Voyager 1 took the northern route and visited neither.
tl.t5_body: Instruments recorded a sharp drop in solar-wind pressure — both probes officially entered interstellar space.
tl.t6_title: Farther than anything humanity has ever built
tl.t6_body: Both probes keep transmitting data about the interstellar medium, cosmic rays and magnetic fields.

rtg.v1Body: Power drops by about 4 W per year. At current estimates, the last science instruments will have to be shut down around 2025–2027, after which the probe will continue flying silently.
rtg.v2Body: NASA engineers have already turned off some heater systems to keep the science instruments running a few more years beyond the original plan.

gold.title: A message for anyone who finds them
gold.num: built to last billions of years
gold.body: Each probe carries a gold-plated copper record with sounds of Earth, music from many cultures and greetings in 55 languages — including Ukrainian.

orbitMap.helioLabel: HELIOPAUSE · edge of the Solar System
orbitMap.hint: Click a milestone dot to learn more

milestones.start: Voyager 2 launched Aug 20, 1977 — 16 days before Voyager 1 (Sep 5, 1977), but on a slower trajectory.
milestones.v1_jupiter: Jupiter flyby in March 1979 — first close-ups of the Great Red Spot and the planet's rings.
milestones.v1_saturn: Saturn flyby in November 1980 — studied the rings and the moon Titan.
milestones.v1_helio: Aug 25, 2012: Voyager 1 became the first craft to cross the heliopause, the solar wind's edge.
milestones.v1_now: The farthest human-made object — over 166 AU from the Sun, in interstellar space.
milestones.v2_jupiter: Jupiter flyby in July 1979 — discovered active volcanoes on the moon Io.
milestones.v2_saturn: Saturn flyby in August 1981 — trajectory bent onward toward Uranus.
milestones.v2_uranus: Uranus flyby in January 1986 — the only close-up images of the planet in history.
milestones.v2_neptune: Neptune flyby in August 1989 — the final planetary encounter, then heading south.
milestones.v2_helio: Nov 5, 2018: Voyager 2 crossed the heliopause, second after Voyager 1.
milestones.v2_now: Over 139 AU from the Sun, sending interstellar data from the southern direction.

hero.title:
RTL-SDR as a real
scientific instrument
hero.sub: For a cheap USB receiver and a simple antenna you can do real science — from receiving Jupiter's radio emission to counting meteors by radio reflection. The data you collect is used by professional observation networks too.

s1.title: Jupiter radio bursts
s1.sub: Jupiter is a powerful source of natural radio emission. The interaction of its magnetosphere with the moon Io creates short pulses (S-bursts) and longer “drifting” bursts (L-bursts) you can hear and see on an ordinary SDR receiver with a simple antenna — no telescope needed.

rtl.spectroCaption: Example waterfall of Jupiter reception, 18–28 MHz

cards.bestTimeFoot: Activity is tied to the position of the moon Io in its orbit
cards.networkFoot: A NASA project where amateurs submit their data

sBurst.title: S-bursts
sBurst.body: Very short pulses (milliseconds) that sound like crackling or “popcorn pops”. They arrive in bursts during active Io passes past specific magnetic field lines of Jupiter.

lBurst.title: L-bursts
lBurst.body: Last from seconds to a few minutes, with a slight frequency drift — they sound like surf or wind noise that rises and falls.

s2.title: Meteor radio monitoring
s2.sub: When a meteor burns up in the atmosphere it leaves a brief ionized trail that can reflect signals from distant transmitters — TV towers, radars or even foreign FM stations. An RTL-SDR pointed at such a distant signal (one normally not received directly due to Earth's curvature) registers short “pings” each time a meteor flies between transmitter and receiver.

rtl.pingCaption: Example recording: quiet background and five reflected “ping” signals from meteors

metCards.rangeFoot: VHF: distant FM/TV stations, GRAVES radars
metCards.measureFoot: Pings per hour — the basis of your own activity statistics
metCards.useFoot: Works during the day and in cloudy weather — unlike visual observing

rtl.showerBody: The number of recorded radio pings correlates well with a shower's peak — you can plot your own activity chart even under a cloudy sky.

gear.p1: A receiver with direct sampling for the HF band — that's what lets it receive Jupiter's 18–28 MHz without an extra converter.
gear.p2: A simple dipole or a magnetic loop antenna tuned to 20 MHz — even a basic build gives acceptable reception.
gear.p3: A directional antenna (Yagi) for your chosen distant transmitter significantly increases the number of recorded pings compared to a simple dipole.
gear.p4: SDR# or GNU Radio for reception and recording; dedicated RadioJOVE software for analyzing and submitting Jupiter observations to the NASA network.
gear.p5: Far from electrical noise sources (power supplies, Wi-Fi routers) — industrial interference often masks faint natural signals.

rtl.communityTitle: Discussing antennas, settings and reception results
rtl.communityBody: OrbitLight members share Jupiter spectrograms, compare meteor ping statistics and help with first SDR setup.

hero.title:
The planets
of the solar system
hero.sub: Eight planets from Mercury to Neptune, side by side. Click Mars for live weather and fresh rover photos; pages for the other planets are on the way.

planetarium.footNote: Pages for the other planets are in the works. Mars is already live with rover and InSight weather data.

blurbs.mercury: Smallest and closest to the Sun — rocky, airless, with a 600 °C swing between day and night.
blurbs.venus: Hottest planet: a runaway greenhouse heated it to +464 °C, worse than Mercury.
blurbs.earth: The only known planet with life and liquid surface water. Our home.
blurbs.mars: The red planet, with a thin atmosphere, two moons and rovers working on it right now.
blurbs.jupiter: Largest planet: a gas giant with the Great Red Spot and over 90 moons.
blurbs.saturn: A gas giant famous for its bright rings of ice and dust.
blurbs.uranus: An ice giant that orbits "on its side" — its axis is tilted 98°.
blurbs.neptune: The farthest planet, deep blue, with the strongest winds in the system.

up close and live

weather.title: Weather on Mars
weather.sub: Latest telemetry from the InSight (NASA) weather station on the surface of Mars — temperature, pressure and wind over the last sol (Martian day).

moons.title: Phobos and Deimos
moons.note: Phases are illustrative (both moons spin too fast for a phase to be a stable trait like our Moon's).
moons.phobosDesc: The larger, closer of the two moons — only 6,000 km above the surface. It spins so fast (once every 7.7 h) that in the Martian sky it rises in the west and sets in the east twice a day. It is slowly falling toward Mars and in roughly 30–50 million years will either crash into the planet or break into a ring.
moons.deimosDesc: The smaller, farther moon, only 12.4 km across. It orbits so slowly relative to Mars' rotation that from the surface its motion across the sky is almost imperceptible — a full lap of the sky takes about two months.

rovers.title: Fresh rover photos
rovers.notConfigured: Mars Vista API key isn't configured server-side — placeholders shown. The feature works once MARS_VISTA_API_KEY is set.

lightbox.desc: A fresh photo from the {{rover}} rover on the surface of Mars. Source: Mars Vista API (NASA/JPL metadata).

route.title: Perseverance route
route.liveNow: mission ongoing · sol counter is live
route.note: Schematic map: shows the documented early Perseverance traverse (sol 0 → 1402). The current sol counter is computed live from the landing date. Exact coordinates and the up-to-date path are on NASA Mars Trek; waypoint positions are refreshed manually before each release.

dust.title: Dust storms
dust.sub: Regional dust storms on Mars most often occur in the southern hemisphere's spring and summer. The 2018 global storm that finally killed the Opportunity rover began in exactly this period.
dust.riskFoot: Regional storms possible in the coming weeks

pressure.title: Pressure like 35 km above Earth
pressure.sub: Mean surface pressure on Mars is about 0.6% of Earth's — roughly what you'd feel at 35 km above Earth without a suit: the fluids in your body would start boiling within seconds.

desc.firstLandings: The first craft to successfully land on Mars and start returning surface images and soil analysis results.
desc.firstRover: The first Mars rover in history — microwave-sized, yet it proved the very concept of mobile planetary exploration.
desc.longevity: Twin rovers with a planned 90-day lifetime — Opportunity worked for over 14 years.
desc.today: A car-sized rover with a nuclear power source — still active in Gale crater.
desc.firstFlight: Ingenuity made the first controlled flight of an aircraft on another planet — 5 flights were planned, it flew over 70.
desc.ahead: A planned return of the samples collected by Perseverance to Earth, followed by the first crewed mission designs.

missions.title: Status of all Mars missions
missions.note: * Ingenuity ended its flights in January 2024 after a rotor-blade damage — Perseverance continues its work

window.title: Next Mars launch window
window.foot: The next launch window is expected to open in early 2027.
window.whyBody: Because Earth and Mars move around the Sun at different speeds, a favourable launch window (least fuel) opens only about once every 26 months — when the planets line up the right way for a Hohmann transfer.

facts.title: Mars of records
facts.olympusFoot: The tallest volcano in the solar system — 2.5× higher than Everest
facts.vallesFoot: A canyon longer than the USA — 10× the length of the Grand Canyon
facts.meteoritesFoot: Fragments of Mars found on Earth — blasted into space by ancient asteroid impacts

hero.title:
Jupiter
and its Galilean moons
hero.sub: The largest planet in the Solar System: the Great Red Spot, four worlds discovered by Galileo in 1610, and a stronger magnetic field than any other body in the system.

stats.note: Distance and signal travel time are live, from the JPL de440s ephemeris.

weather.title: Jupiter's atmosphere right now
weather.grsFoot: Continues to slowly shrink every year
weather.windFoot: At the spot's edge — the most powerful storm in the system
weather.tempFoot: Top of the visible ammonia clouds

moons.title: Moons of Jupiter
moons.sub: Jupiter has {{count}} known moons — most are small and irregularly shaped. Here are the eight shown in the animation above: four tiny ring moons closest to the planet and the four large Galilean moons.
moons.note: The orbital periods of Io, Europa and Ganymede are locked in a 1:2:4 resonance (Laplace resonance) — which is why their mutual gravity keeps Io volcanically active

metis.name: Metis
metis.desc: One of the closest moons to Jupiter — it orbits faster than the planet rotates on its axis.

adrastea.name: Adrastea
adrastea.desc: A tiny irregularly shaped moon, likely the source of material for Jupiter's thin ring.

amalthea.name: Amalthea
amalthea.desc: A reddish surface dusted with sulfur from Io's volcanoes — it emits more heat than it receives from the Sun.

thebe.name: Thebe
thebe.desc: The farthest of the four inner moons, with the large Zethus crater on its surface.

io.name: Io
io.desc: The most volcanic body in the Solar System — over 400 active volcanoes, heated by Jupiter's tidal forces.

europa.name: Europa
europa.desc: An icy world with a subsurface ocean of liquid water — the prime candidate in the search for extraterrestrial life.

ganymede.name: Ganymede
ganymede.desc: The largest moon in the Solar System — bigger than Mercury, the only moon with its own magnetic field.

callisto.name: Callisto
callisto.desc: The most heavily cratered object in the Solar System — its surface has been unchanged for billions of years.

system.title: The full moon system of Jupiter
system.sub: Six dynamical groups of Jupiter's moons — from the ring group near the planet to the distant irregulars. Prograde (with rotation) in teal, retrograde in coral. Hover a moon for details.
system.scaleNote: Orbits are drawn on a true linear scale using real semi-major axes: from 128 thousand km (Metis) to ~24 million km (outer irregulars) — a ~190× span, so the inner 8 moons cluster tightly near the planet and the distant ones sit at the periphery. This is the real architecture of the system. Orbits are Keplerian: real eccentricity and variable speed per Kepler's 2nd law (faster near perihelion, slower near aphelion) with Jupiter at the ellipse focus. Time is sped up for clarity (1 s ≈ 0.1 days); relative speeds are real. The ellipse orientation is approximate (JPL mean elements omit the argument of perihelion, so it is derived deterministically from the name), and orbital inclination is not shown. Current phase is approximate. Deep zoom and detail cards — in the fullscreen viewer.
system.fullscreenHint: Open the fullscreen explorer — deep zoom, real moon photos and a detail card for every one of the {{count}} moons
system.noPhotoBody: This object is known only as a point of light in telescopes — no high-resolution image exists.

grs.title: The Great Red Spot is shrinking
grs.sub: The most famous storm in the Solar System has been steadily shrinking for over a century of observations — the cause of this process is still not fully understood.

depth.title: What happens if you dive in
depth.sub: Jupiter has no surface to land on — only a gradual transition from gas to liquid under rising pressure and temperature.
depth.m1: ~1000 km · pressure like the bottom of Earth's ocean
depth.m3: ~13,000 km · metallic hydrogen, source of the magnetic field

radiation.title: Radiation environment
radiation.note: For comparison: a lethal dose for a human is about 5 Gy at once. This is why spacecraft near Jupiter need thick titanium shielding.

opposition.title: Next Jupiter opposition
opposition.until: Until the best time to observe
opposition.foot: At opposition Jupiter is brightest and visible all night
opposition.whatBody: About every 13 months Earth passes directly between the Sun and Jupiter — the planet rises in the east right after sunset and stays visible all night, reaching maximum brightness.
opposition.passed: Jupiter is at opposition right now — the best time to observe!

facts.magneticFoot: The most powerful magnetic field of any planet in the Solar System
facts.starFoot: If Jupiter were 80 times more massive, fusion would ignite inside it

hero.title:
Mercury
world of extremes
hero.sub: The closest and fastest planet to the Sun: no atmosphere, no moons, extreme temperature variations, and a strange 3:2 spin-orbit resonance.

orbit.title: Mercury's eccentric orbit
orbit.desc1: Mercury has the most eccentric orbit of any major planet in the Solar System, with an eccentricity of 0.206. Its distance to the Sun varies by nearly double: ranging from 46 million kilometers at its closest point (perihelion) to 70 million kilometers at its farthest (aphelion).
orbit.desc2: This highly elongated orbit causes the planet's speed to fluctuate significantly, from 39 km/s near aphelion to almost 59 km/s near perihelion. For scale, Earth's orbit shown on the scheme is almost perfectly circular (eccentricity of just 0.017).
orbit.footnote: Mercury's orbit is the most eccentric among all planets (0.206): its distance to the Sun changes by nearly double during a single revolution.

weather.title: Mercury right now
weather.speedFoot: Fastest planet in the Solar System
weather.dayFoot: Longer than a mercury year (88 days)
weather.atmosFoot: Only a tenuous exosphere of Na, K, O, He

resonance.title: 3:2 spin-orbit resonance
resonance.p1: Mercury is the only major planet in the Solar System with a confirmed 3:2 spin-orbit resonance: for every two orbits around the Sun, it rotates on its axis exactly three times. This is a result of the Sun's gravitational tidal forces acting on the planet's eccentric orbit and non-spherical shape.
resonance.p2: Due to this coupling of rotation and orbit, a single point on Mercury's surface sees a sunrise only once every 176 Earth days. Near perihelion, an observer on Mercury would see the Sun rise, stop, reverse direction, and then resume its forward journey across the sky.

temperature.eyebrow: Largest temp swing in the system
temperature.title: From +430°C to −180°C
temperature.sub: Without an atmosphere to retain heat, Mercury's day side gets hotter than almost any other planet, while the night side plunges to the lowest temperatures. Paradoxically, water ice exists in permanently shadowed craters at the poles.

surface.title: Caloris Basin & Surface Features
surface.c1Desc: Caloris Basin is one of the largest impact basins in the entire Solar System. The image was captured by NASA's MESSENGER spacecraft.
surface.c2Desc: Lobate scarps (rupes) are giant cliffs hundreds of kilometers long, formed by thrust faults as the planet's core cooled and contracted.
surface.c3Desc: Polar crater is a permanently shadowed zone at Mercury's poles where radar measurements from MESSENGER confirmed deposits of water ice.
surface.c4Desc: Enhanced color mosaic of Mercury's surface created by combining MESSENGER filters to highlight geological and chemical differences of rocks.
surface.basinfoot: One of the largest impact basins in the Solar System
surface.shrinkfoot: Radius shrunk as the core cooled — creating 'wrinkles' (rupes)
surface.corefoot: Occupies most of the radius — largest relative core of any planet

missions.title: Missions to Mercury
missions.footnote: BepiColombo performed six gravity assists at Mercury before entering permanent orbit — flying to the innermost planet paradoxically requires deceleration rather than acceleration due to the Sun's strong gravity.

observe.title: Best times for observation
observe.whyK: Why Mercury is hard to see
observe.whyBody: Mercury never departs more than 28° from the Sun in our sky. Therefore, it can only be spotted in a brief window just after sunset or before sunrise, and only a few times a year during greatest elongations.
observe.footEastern: Best visibility above the western horizon immediately after sunset
observe.footWestern: Best visibility above the eastern horizon immediately before sunrise

facts.title: Mercury of Records
facts.speedFoot: Hence the name after the swift messenger of the gods
facts.moonsFoot: Along with Venus — the only planets without natural satellites
facts.transitFoot: A rare phenomenon — happens only 13-14 times per century

hero.title: Famous galaxies
hero.sub: From our own Milky Way to the Cartwheel ring galaxy half a billion light-years away — twelve of the most famous galaxies in the universe with real distances, types and scales.

localGroup.title: The Local Group
localGroup.sub: A gravitationally bound cluster of galaxies that includes the Milky Way, Andromeda and the Triangulum Galaxy, along with dozens of smaller satellite galaxies within about 10 million light-years.

distances.title: How far away they are
distances.sub: Distances are given in light-years; on a logarithmic scale, because the difference between the nearest and the farthest spans many orders of magnitude, and only a log axis can show them all at once.

records.title: Galactic champions
records.brightestFoot: The lower the magnitude, the brighter the galaxy

galaxy.gallerySub: Photos from Wikimedia Commons and the NASA Image Library.
galaxy.skyPosSub: Where to find the galaxy on the night sky
galaxy.zoomOut: Click to zoom out · drag to pan
galaxy.zoomHint: Scroll to zoom · drag to pan

hero.eyebrow: Third planet · the only known with life
hero.title:
Earth
our island in space
hero.sub: The only known planet with liquid water on the surface, an oxygen-rich atmosphere, plate tectonics, and life. Everything you have ever seen, except for a few hundred people in orbit, happened right here.
hero.lightTimeL: light travel time from the Sun

stats.title: Earth right now
stats.populationFoot: Continues to grow, growth rate is slowing
stats.speedFoot: You are moving this fast right now
stats.fieldFoot: Protects against solar wind and cosmic radiation
stats.periodFoot: Sidereal day — slightly shorter than the usual 24-hour day

r.tectonicsC: Venus and Mars — single continuous crust
r.oxygenC: result of billions of years of photosynthesis
r.moonSizeC: largest ratio among planets with satellites
r.magnetosphereC: Mars and Venus have practically lost it

seasons.title: Axial tilt 23.4°
seasons.p1: Earth's axis of rotation is tilted by 23.4° relative to its orbital plane — this tilt, rather than the distance to the Sun, causes the seasons. When the Northern Hemisphere is tilted toward the Sun, it experiences summer, while the Southern Hemisphere experiences winter.
seasons.p2: The tilt slowly varies between 22.1° and 24.5° in cycles of approximately 41,000 years (Milankovitch cycles) — one of the factors driving long-term climate cycles, including ice ages.

interior.title: What is under our feet
interior.sub: Earth consists of four main layers — from a thin solid crust to a hot iron core, whose rotation creates the planet's magnetic field.
interior.m3: 2,890–5,150 km · outer core, liquid iron-nickel, source of the magnetic field
interior.m4: 5,150–6,371 km · inner core, solid despite high heat — holds under pressure
interior.m5: Center · ~5,400°C — almost as hot as the Sun's surface

atmosphere.title: Atmospheric layers
atmosphere.sub: A thin envelope of gas only a few hundred kilometers thick separates Earth's surface from the vacuum of space — and it is where everything we call weather occurs.
atmosphere.m2: 85–600 km · thermosphere, where ISS orbits (~400 km)
atmosphere.m3: 50–85 km · mesosphere, where meteors burn up
atmosphere.m5: 0–12 km · troposphere, where all weather forms

magnetosphere.title: Magnetosphere & aurora
magnetosphere.sourceFoot: Rotation of molten iron and nickel creates a geodynamo
magnetosphere.protectFoot: Without the magnetosphere, the atmosphere would gradually be stripped away, like Mars
magnetosphere.auroraFoot: Charged particles directed to the poles excite the atmosphere
magnetosphere.note: Live aurora and space weather forecast — on the page

moonRel.title: The Moon is slowly escaping, and the day is lengthening
moonRel.recedeBody: Tidal friction gradually transfers Earth's rotational energy to the Moon, causing it to recede by about 3.8 cm per year — roughly the speed at which fingernails grow.
moonRel.dayBody: The same process slows down Earth's rotation — the day lengthens by about 1.8 milliseconds per century. 600 million years ago, a day was only about 21 hours long.

observation.title: Earth observation satellites
observation.note: More details on the ISS and live pass tracking — on the page
observation.s2_detail: Lagrange point L1 · solar wind monitoring

records.title: Earth of records
records.c1_foot: The densest of all planets in the Solar System
records.c2_foot: Small asteroids are sometimes temporarily captured by Earth's gravity for months or years
records.c3_foot: The ocean floor is constantly being renewed along mid-ocean ridges

climate.title: Earth's Climate Health
climate.co2Foot: Atmospheric concentration, highest in 3 million years
climate.tempFoot: Deviation from the baseline global average
climate.seaLevelFoot: Rise of the global ocean level since 1993

seismic.title: Latest strong earthquake on the planet

hero.title:
Venus
hell under clouds
hero.sub: The brightest object in the night sky after the Moon and the hottest planet in the Solar System — despite Mercury being closer to the Sun. The culprit is a runaway greenhouse effect in a dense atmosphere of carbon dioxide.
hero.orbitLabel: Venus' orbit · 108 million km, almost a perfect circle
hero.footnote: Venus' orbit is the roundest of all planets (eccentricity only 0.007) and the closest approach to Earth among all planets in the Solar System

stats.title: Venus right now
stats.tempFoot: Hotter than Mercury, despite greater distance to the Sun
stats.pressureFoot: Like at a depth of 900 m in Earth's ocean
stats.speedFoot: The atmosphere rotates 60 times faster than the planet itself
stats.periodFoot: Slowest and in the reverse direction

compare.title: "Sister" in size only
compare.footnote: In size, mass, and gravity, Venus is indeed similar to Earth — which is why it is called our "twin sister". But the similarity ends there.

retrograde.title: Rotates in the opposite direction
retrograde.svgLabel: Comparison of rotation directions and axial tilts
retrograde.p1: If you look at the Solar System from above Earth's North Pole, almost all planets rotate around their axis counterclockwise — the same direction they move in their orbits. Venus is the exception: it rotates clockwise, in the opposite direction.
retrograde.p2: The most likely cause is a massive collision during the early stages of the planet's formation that literally flipped its rotation. As a result, the Sun on Venus rises in the west and sets in the east — if it could be seen through the dense clouds at all with the naked eye from the surface.

greenhouse.title: Through sulfuric acid clouds to the surface
greenhouse.sub: 96.5% carbon dioxide in the atmosphere traps heat so effectively that the surface is hotter than that of Mercury, which is three times closer to the Sun. This is the most striking example of a runaway greenhouse effect in the Solar System — and a warning for understanding Earth's climate.
greenhouse.m1: 70 km · tops of sulfuric acid clouds, −45°C
greenhouse.m2: 50 km · "habitable" temperature zone (+27°C), but acid clouds

surface.title: Volcanic surface under the clouds
surface.sub: Optical cameras cannot see the surface of Venus through the continuous cloud layer — all relief maps are obtained by radar, which "sees through" the atmosphere.
surface.p1Desc: Global radar mosaic of Venus compiled from Magellan data. Colors simulate hues recorded by Soviet Venera 13 and 14 landers.
surface.p2Desc: 3D computer-generated perspective of the 8 km high volcano Maat Mons, reconstructed from Magellan radar data.
surface.p3Desc: High-altitude plateau of Lakshmi Planum and folded mountain ranges of Maxwell Montes, located in the northern hemisphere.
surface.p4Desc: Mead crater is the largest impact crater on Venus, with a diameter of about 280 km and a double-ring structure.
surface.volcanoesFoot: More than on any other planet in the Solar System

missions.title: Missions to Venus
missions.footnote: The longest-surviving spacecraft on Venus' surface was Venera 13 — 127 minutes, before heat and pressure disabled the electronics.

observe.title: The brightest now in the sky
observe.phasesBody: Through a telescope, Venus displays phases similar to the Moon's — from a thin crescent to a nearly full disc. Galileo's observation of these phases in 1610 was one of the first direct proofs in favor of Copernicus' heliocentric model.

records.title: Venus of records
records.c1_foot: Third brightest object in the sky after the Sun and Moon
records.c2_foot: Pairs of transits occur once every 100+ years
records.c3_foot: Rotation around its axis lasts longer than its orbit around the Sun

hero.eyebrow: Eighth planet · farthest · updated just now
hero.title:
Neptune
found by calculation
hero.sub: The only planet discovered by math rather than direct observation — its position was predicted from perturbations in Uranus's orbit before it was ever seen in a telescope. The windiest planet in the Solar System, with a single large retrograde moon.
hero.footnote: Triton (marked ↺) is the only large moon in the Solar System that orbits in the opposite direction of its planet's rotation.

weather.title: Neptune right now
weather.speedFoot: The strongest winds of any planet in the Solar System
weather.tempFoot: The planet radiates twice as much heat as it receives from the Sun
weather.rotFoot: Similar to Jupiter and Saturn, despite its icy composition
weather.revFoot: Since Neptune was discovered in 1846 — just one Neptunian year ago

discovery.title: A planet found on paper
discovery.p1: Neptune is the only planet in the Solar System discovered by mathematical prediction rather than by chance observation. Astronomers Urbain Le Verrier and John Couch Adams independently calculated where the unknown planet should be by analyzing perturbations in Uranus's orbit.
discovery.p2: Johann Galle at the Berlin Observatory pointed his telescope at the calculated sky position and found the planet that same night, less than one degree from the predicted location.
discovery.timeFoot: Neptune has completed just over one full orbit around the Sun since then

darkSpot.title: Disappearing dark spots
darkSpot.sub: Voyager 2 photographed the Great Dark Spot in 1989—a storm the size of Earth. But when the Hubble Space Telescope observed it in 1994, the spot had vanished. Since then, new dark spots have appeared and faded, unlike the centuries-long stability of Jupiter's Great Red Spot.

c1.title: Discovered
c1.foot: By Voyager 2 during its only flyby of Neptune

c2.title: Disappeared
c2.foot: Confirmed by the Hubble Space Telescope

c3.title: Storm duration
c3.foot: Unlike the hundreds of years of Jupiter's spot

rings.title: Five faint rings
rings.sub: Galle, Le Verrier, Lassell, Arago, and Adams rings—faint and dusty, with unusual clumps ("arcs") in the Adams ring, whose stability is still not fully explained by gravitational models.

galle.name: Galle Ring
galle.desc: The innermost, broad and faint ring named after Johann Gottfried Galle, who first observed Neptune in 1846.

leverrier.name: Le Verrier Ring
leverrier.desc: A narrow ring named after Urbain Le Verrier. Coincides with the orbit of the moon Despina, which acts as a shepherd moon.

lassell.name: Lassell Ring
lassell.desc: The widest ring in the system, named after William Lassell. It is a broad, faint sheet of dust stretching between Le Verrier and Arago.

arago.name: Arago Ring
arago.desc: A narrow, faint ring named after François Arago, located just outside the Lassell ring and inside the Adams ring.

adams.name: Adams Ring
adams.desc: The outermost, best-studied ring named after John Couch Adams. It contains five distinct bright clumps of dust called arcs.

triton.title: Triton: captured and doomed

c1.title: Retrograde orbit
c1.foot: Orbits in the opposite direction of Neptune's rotation—strong evidence that it is a captured Kuiper Belt object

c2.title: Cryovolcanoes
c2.foot: Voyager 2 photographed active eruptions of freezing nitrogen

c3.title: Future
c3.foot: Tidal forces will gradually drag Triton inward until it breaks apart into a new ring

triton.footnote: Triton's surface is one of the coldest measured in the Solar System, at approximately -235°C

moons.title: Neptune's complete moon system
moons.sub: Besides Triton, Neptune hosts seven tiny moons among the rings, eccentric Nereid on a strange elongated orbit, and seven outer irregular moons—mostly captured objects in retrograde orbits.
moons.sub_block: Aside from the massive retrograde Triton, Neptune is orbited by a family of small inner moons within its rings and distant irregular satellites.
moons.note: Triton contains 99.5% of the mass of all Neptune's satellites and rings, highlighting its unique outer-system origin.

naiad.name: Naiad
naiad.desc: Neptune's innermost moon. Its orbit is so low that tidal forces will eventually pull it apart into a new ring.

thalassa.name: Thalassa
thalassa.desc: Orbits extremely close to Naiad in a unique orbital resonance that maintains their separation.

despina.name: Despina
despina.desc: Located within Neptune's faint rings, acting as a shepherd moon stabilizing the Le Verrier ring.

galatea.name: Galatea
galatea.desc: Interacts gravitationally with the outermost Adams ring, shaping its dust clumps and arcs.

larissa.name: Larissa
larissa.desc: An irregular, heavily cratered moon, originally discovered during a stellar occultation in 1981.

proteus.name: Proteus
proteus.desc: Neptune's second largest moon, shaped like an irregular polyhedron—the size limit for non-spherical bodies.

triton.name: Triton
triton.desc: An icy world with cryovolcanoes and a nitrogen atmosphere. Orbits retrograde, proving its Kuiper Belt capture.

nereid.name: Nereid
nereid.desc: Possesses one of the most eccentric orbits in the Solar System, swinging out as far as 9.6 million km.

c2.title: Offset from center
c2.foot: Like Uranus, both ice giants share this unique feature

c3.title: Possible cause
c3.foot: Not a deep metallic core like gas giants, but a mantle of ionic "oceanic" water and ammonia

missions.eyebrow: Who explored and plans to explore
missions.title: Missions to Neptune
missions.v2st: The only direct data on the planet, rings, and Triton
missions.footnote: Everything known about Neptune from direct observations was obtained during one day of Voyager 2's single flyby in August 1989—the final stop of the probe's "Grand Tour".

opposition.title: Neptune's next opposition
opposition.foot: Telescope required—not visible to the naked eye
opposition.findBody: Neptune's magnitude is around 7.8m, which is twice as faint as the naked-eye limit. You will need binoculars or a small telescope and a precise star map to find it in Aquarius or neighboring constellations.

system.title: Neptune's complete moon system
system.sub: Four dynamic groups of Neptune's moons — from inner ring group near the planet to distant irregulars. Prograde moons are teal, retrograde are coral. Hover for details.
system.scaleNote: Orbits are drawn to true linear scale by real semi-major axes: from 48k km (Naiad) to ~50M km (outer irregulars) — a ~1000x span, so the inner moons cluster tightly near the planet. Time is sped up (1s ≈ 0.1 days); relative speeds are real. Orbits are Keplerian: real eccentricity and variable speed. Deep zoom is available in the fullscreen viewer.

records.title: Neptune of records
records.c1_foot: After Pluto was excluded from the list of planets in 2006
records.c2_foot: Solar System record, despite minimum solar energy
records.c3_foot: Predicted by calculations before the first observation

hero.title:
Uranus
the rolling planet
hero.sub: The only planet in the Solar System whose axis of rotation is tilted so far that it actually lies on its side. An ice giant with the coldest atmosphere in the system—even colder than the more distant Neptune.
hero.footnote: Due to the extreme tilt of Uranus's rotation axis, its rings and moon orbits lie nearly perpendicular to the plane of the Solar System.

weather.title: Uranus right now
weather.speedFoot: The coldest atmosphere among all planets in the system
weather.tempFoot: The planet rotates practically "lying on its side"
weather.rotFoot: In the retrograde direction due to axial tilt
weather.revFoot: Water, ammonia, and methane over a rocky core—not a gas giant

tilt.title: Why Uranus lies on its side
tilt.p1: Most planets have moderately tilted rotation axes (like Earth's 23.4°). Uranus is the exception: its tilt is 97.7°, meaning its axis of rotation lies almost in its orbital plane. The most likely cause is a catastrophic collision with a Earth-sized body during the planet's early formation stages.
tilt.p2: The result is extreme seasons: each pole receives 42 years of continuous sunlight, followed by 42 years of complete darkness. The rings and moons orbit in the same tilted plane, which is why they appear nearly vertical to us.

rings.title: Faint vertical rings
rings.sub: Uranus's rings were not discovered directly by telescope, but through stellar occultation—while observing Uranus pass in front of a distant star, astronomers noticed brief eclipses before and after the planet itself passed.

zeta.name: Zeta Ring
zeta.desc: The closest broad, extremely faint dust ring surrounding Uranus.

ring6.name: Ring 6
ring6.desc: The innermost narrow ring, the first of three numbered rings found during stellar occultation.

ring5.name: Ring 5
ring5.desc: The second of the numbered rings. Very narrow and faint, located between Ring 6 and Ring 4.

ring4.name: Ring 4
ring4.desc: The third of the numbered rings. Features sharp edges and low dust content.

alpha.name: Alpha Ring
alpha.desc: One of the most distinct inner rings of Uranus, found among the planet's first nine rings.

beta.name: Beta Ring
beta.desc: A bright inner ring, similar in structure and width to the neighboring Alpha Ring.

eta.name: Eta Ring
eta.desc: A complex ring system containing a narrow, bright core and a wide, faint dust sheet.

gamma.name: Gamma Ring
gamma.desc: A very narrow and bright ring with low dust content and high particle density.

delta.name: Delta Ring
delta.desc: A circular ring showing pronounced brightness asymmetry, indicating uneven material distribution.

lambda.name: Lambda Ring
lambda.desc: A thin and faint dust ring located just inside the prominent Epsilon Ring.

epsilon.name: Epsilon Ring
epsilon.desc: The brightest, widest, and densest ring of Uranus. Its width varies from 20 to 100 km along its orbit.

nu.name: Nu Ring
nu.desc: A broad, reddish outer ring located in the orbital zone of the small moon Portia.

mu.name: Mu Ring
mu.desc: The outermost broad, blue dust ring, whose material is supplied by the tiny moon Mab.

moons.title: Complete moon system of Uranus
moons.sub: Besides the five major moons, Uranus hosts 13 tiny moons among the rings and another 10 distant irregular retrograde moons—likely asteroids captured by Uranus's gravity.
moons.sub_block: Uranus is surrounded by 28 moons: from inner ring moons to the big five Shakespearean worlds and distant irregular bodies.
moons.note: All moons of Uranus are named after characters from the works of William Shakespeare and Alexander Pope.

miranda.name: Miranda
miranda.desc: Features a chaotic surface with Verona Rupes cliff ~20 km high. The surface looks like it was stitched from different pieces.

ariel.name: Ariel
ariel.desc: The brightest moon of Uranus, with a network of deep canyons—signs of ancient geological activity.

umbriel.name: Umbriel
umbriel.desc: The darkest of the major moons, heavily cratered—geologically the quietest of the five.

titania.name: Titania
titania.desc: Uranus's largest moon, with giant canyons. It might host a thin subsurface water mantle.

oberon.name: Oberon
oberon.desc: The outermost of the major moons, covered in ancient craters—there are signs of past cryovolcanism on the surface.

c1.title: Field tilt angle
c1.foot: Relative to the rotation axis—highly skewed

c2.title: Offset from center
c2.foot: The magnetic field does not pass through the center of the planet

c3.title: Magnetosphere shape
c3.foot: Due to rotation and tilt, the magnetic tail twists behind the planet

opposition.title: Uranus's next opposition
opposition.foot: On the limit of naked-eye visibility under a very dark sky
opposition.findBody: Uranus has a magnitude of about 5.7m—theoretically visible to the naked eye under perfectly dark skies, but for confident observation you will need binoculars and a detailed finder chart.

system.title: Complete moon system of Uranus
system.sub: Three dynamic groups of Uranus's moons—from inner ring moons to the major moons and distant irregulars. Prograde are teal, retrograde are coral. Hover for details.
system.scaleNote: Orbits are drawn to true linear scale based on semi-major axes: from 49k km (Cordelia) to ~20M km (outer irregulars)—a difference of ~400x. Time is accelerated (1s ≈ 0.1 days). Deep zoom is available in the fullscreen viewer.

records.c1_foot: William Herschel—first planet found by telescope
records.c2_foot: Colder than Neptune, although further from the Sun

hero.title:
Saturn
lord of the rings
hero.sub: The planet with the most spectacular rings. Although other gas giants have rings, Saturn's are made mostly of water ice and reflect sunlight beautifully.
hero.footnote: Titan (marked on the diagram) is the only moon in the Solar System with a dense atmosphere; the moons shown are only a fraction of the {{count}}+ known

weather.eyebrow: A legacy of the Cassini mission
weather.title: Saturn right now
weather.speedFoot: Among the fastest winds in the Solar System
weather.tempFoot: Upper boundary of the visible ammonia clouds
weather.revFoot: The axial tilt is why the rings appear wide open, then nearly edge-on

rings.eyebrow: The most spectacular in the system
rings.title: What the rings are made of
rings.sub: Saturn's rings stretch from ~7,000 to ~80,000 km above the cloud tops, yet are mostly less than a kilometer thick — if Saturn were shrunk to the size of a football, the rings would be thinner than a sheet of paper.

c1.title: Composition
c1.foot: Plus traces of rock and dust

c2.title: Thickness
c2.foot: Across a diameter of over 270,000 km

c3.title: Origin
c3.foot: Debris from a shattered moon, or primordial material — debate continues

d.name: D Ring
d.desc: Closest to the planet — an extremely faint, almost transparent ring only visible in long-exposure images.

c.name: C Ring
c.desc: The semi-transparent "Crepe Ring" — darker and thinner than the neighboring B and A rings; the planet's disc shows through it.

b.name: B Ring
b.desc: The widest and brightest ring in the system — it holds most of the mass of all of Saturn's rings.

cassini.name: Cassini Division
cassini.desc: A dark, nearly 5,000 km-wide gap between the B and A rings, swept clear by an orbital resonance with the moon Mimas.

a.name: A Ring
a.desc: The outer of the two great bright rings — it contains the Encke Gap, patrolled by the tiny shepherd moon Pan.

f.name: F Ring
f.desc: A narrow, strange ring with a braided, kinked structure — shaped by the shepherd moons Prometheus and Pandora.

g.name: G Ring
g.desc: A faint dust ring fed by particles knocked off the tiny moon Aegaeon.

hexagon.title: Hexagonal Storm
hexagon.desc1: A giant persistent storm in the shape of a perfect hexagon rages at Saturn's north pole. Its diameter is about 30,000 km — two Earths could fit inside.
hexagon.desc2: This is a unique phenomenon in the Solar System. It is thought to be a standing wave in the atmosphere caused by the difference in wind speeds at different latitudes. Winds at its edges reach 320 km/h.

moons.sub_block: From the dense ice ball Mimas to the atmosphere-wrapped Titan — eight moons that shaped how we picture Saturn's system.
moons.note: Titan is the only moon in the Solar System with a dense atmosphere (1.45× denser than Earth's), with lakes and seas of liquid methane and ethane on its surface

mimas.name: Mimas
mimas.desc: The huge Herschel crater makes it look like the 'Death Star' — nearly a third of the moon's own diameter.

enceladus.name: Enceladus
enceladus.desc: Icy geysers at the south pole spray water vapor from a subsurface ocean — directly feeding Saturn's E ring.

tethys.name: Tethys
tethys.desc: An icy moon scarred by the giant Ithaca Chasma canyon, which runs three-quarters of the way around it.

dione.name: Dione
dione.desc: 'Wispy terrain' on its trailing hemisphere creates bright streaks visible from a distance.

rhea.name: Rhea
rhea.desc: Saturn's second-largest moon, heavily cratered — it may even have a faint dust ring of its own.

titan.name: Titan
titan.desc: The only moon with a dense atmosphere — with lakes and seas of liquid methane and ethane on its surface.

hyperion.name: Hyperion
hyperion.desc: A porous, 'sponge-like' shape and chaotic, unpredictable rotation — unique among the large moons.

iapetus.name: Iapetus
iapetus.desc: A two-toned moon — one hemisphere dark as coal, the other bright as snow. The cause is still not fully settled.

system.title: The full system of Saturn's moons
system.sub: From the dense group of moons inside the rings to a huge cloud of small retrograde satellites in distant orbits.
system.fullscreenTitle: The full system of Saturn's moons

c1.title: Axial alignment
c1.foot: The only planet with an almost perfectly axisymmetric field — a puzzle for dynamo theory

c2.title: Field strength
c2.foot: Much weaker than Jupiter's, but stronger than Earth's

c3.title: Magnetosphere
c3.foot: Shaped by interaction with the rings and Titan

missions.eyebrow: Who has explored and who is exploring
missions.title: Missions to Saturn
missions.footnote: The Huygens probe, released from Cassini, made the first and still only landing on a moon in the outer Solar System — on Titan, in January 2005.

opposition.title: Next Saturn opposition
opposition.foot: At opposition, Saturn is visible all night and at its brightest
opposition.telescope_label: What to see through a telescope
opposition.telescope_desc: The rings are clearly visible even in a small telescope from 50× magnification. Under good conditions, you can see the Cassini division in the rings and the largest moon Titan as a tiny star nearby.

c1.title: Least dense planet
c1.foot: The only planet in the Solar System lighter than water

c3.title: Titan's weather cycle
c3.foot: The only other body in the Solar System with stable surface liquids
